subject: Mathematics
name: Mathematics, Level 10A
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: Mathematics, Level 10A

points.title: Surds
points.brief: A surd is a root that cannot be simplified to a rational number, such as √2 or ∛5, while √9 = 3 is not a surd.

points.title: Simplifying surds
points.brief: Take out the largest square factor, such as √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2.

points.title: Adding, subtracting and multiplying surds
points.brief: Only like surds can be added or subtracted, such as 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2, while √a × √b = √(ab).

points.title: Rationalising the denominator
points.brief: Multiply the top and bottom by the surd in the denominator so it becomes rational, such as 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3.

points.title: Fractional indices
points.brief: A fractional index means a root, so a^(1/n) is the nth root of a and a^(m/n) is that root raised to the power m, such as 8^(2/3) = 4.

points.title: What a logarithm is
points.brief: A logarithm is an index. log₂ 8 = 3 because 2³ = 8, so logarithms and exponentials undo each other.

points.title: Laws of logarithms
points.brief: Logs of a product add, logs of a quotient subtract, and a power comes out the front, so log(a³) = 3 log a.

points.title: Solving exponential equations with logarithms
points.brief: When the bases cannot be matched, take logs of both sides, such as 3ˣ = 20 giving x = log 20 ÷ log 3.

points.title: Polynomials and their degree
points.brief: A polynomial is a sum of terms with whole-number powers of x. Its degree is the highest power, and the leading coefficient goes with it.

points.title: The remainder theorem
points.brief: When P(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is P(a), so substituting gives the remainder without dividing.

points.title: The factor theorem
points.brief: If P(a) = 0, then (x - a) is a factor of P(x), which helps factorise a cubic by testing small whole numbers.

points.title: Sketching cubics from factors
points.brief: The factors give the x-intercepts, the constant term gives the y-intercept, and the sign of the x³ term sets which way the curve ends.

points.title: Factorising non-monic quadratics
points.brief: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, split the middle term, and factorise in pairs.

points.title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
points.brief: x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / 2a solves any quadratic, and b² - 4ac tells whether there are two, one or no real solutions.

points.title: Function notation
points.brief: f(x) names a rule, and f(3) means the output when the input is 3, such as f(x) = 2x + 1 giving f(3) = 7.

points.title: Where a line meets a parabola
points.brief: Substitute the line into the quadratic and solve, giving two, one or no points where they meet.

points.title: Turning point form of a parabola
points.brief: y = a(x - h)² + k has its turning point at (h, k), and completing the square puts a quadratic into this form.

points.title: Hyperbolas and asymptotes
points.brief: y = a/(x - h) + k is a hyperbola with a vertical asymptote at x = h and a horizontal asymptote at y = k.

points.title: Equations of circles
points.brief: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r² is a circle with centre (h, k) and radius r.

points.title: Transforming exponential graphs
points.brief: y = aˣ passes through (0, 1) with the x-axis as an asymptote, and adding k moves the asymptote to y = k.

points.title: Volume of pyramids and cones
points.brief: A pyramid or cone holds one third of the prism or cylinder with the same base and height, V = ⅓Ah.

points.title: Surface area of a cone
points.brief: The curved surface is πrs, where s is the slant height, so a closed cone has SA = πr² + πrs.

points.title: Surface area and volume of a sphere
points.brief: A sphere's surface area is 4πr² and its volume is (4/3)πr³.

points.title: Average rate of change
points.brief: The gradient of the line between two points on a curve. As the points move closer, it approaches the rate of change at a single point.

points.title: Angle at the centre and the circumference
points.brief: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.

points.title: Angles in a semicircle and the same segment
points.brief: An angle in a semicircle is 90°, and angles standing on the same arc in the same segment are equal.

points.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
points.brief: A quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle has opposite angles that add to 180°.

points.title: Tangents to a circle
points.brief: A tangent meets the radius at 90°, and two tangents drawn from the same outside point are equal in length.

points.title: Chords and the centre
points.brief: A line from the centre perpendicular to a chord cuts it in half, and equal chords are the same distance from the centre.

points.title: The sine rule
points.brief: In any triangle, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, used when you know a side and its opposite angle.

points.title: The cosine rule
points.brief: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C, used with two sides and the angle between them, or with all three sides to find an angle.

points.title: Area of a triangle with sine
points.brief: Area is half the product of two sides times the sine of the angle between them, ½ab sin C.

points.title: Trigonometry in three dimensions
points.brief: Find a right-angled triangle inside a 3D shape, such as a box's diagonal, and use Pythagoras and trigonometry step by step.

chapters.title: The unit circle and trigonometric graphs

points.title: The unit circle
points.brief: For an angle on a circle of radius 1, the point's x-coordinate is the cosine and its y-coordinate is the sine, which defines them for any angle.

points.title: Graphs of sine and cosine
points.brief: y = sin x and y = cos x are waves between -1 and 1 that repeat every 360°, with cosine starting at its highest point.

points.title: The graph of tangent
points.brief: y = tan x repeats every 180° and has vertical asymptotes at 90°, 270° and so on, where cosine is zero.

points.title: Solving simple trigonometric equations
points.brief: An equation such as sin x = 0.5 has more than one solution from 0° to 360°, found with the calculator and the unit circle's symmetry.

points.title: Standard deviation
points.brief: Standard deviation measures how far values typically sit from the mean. A larger one means the data is more spread out.

points.title: Outliers and standard deviation
points.brief: Because it uses every value, standard deviation grows a lot with one outlier, just as the mean is pulled towards it.

points.title: Choosing a measure of spread
points.brief: Standard deviation suits symmetric data without outliers. The interquartile range suits skewed data or data with outliers.

points.title: Interpolation and extrapolation
points.brief: Predicting with a fitted line inside the range of the data is interpolation and fairly safe. Going beyond it is extrapolation and less reliable.

points.title: The multiplication principle
points.brief: If one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, together there are m × n ways, such as 3 shirts and 4 pants giving 12 outfits.

points.title: Factorial notation
points.brief: n! is the product of every whole number from n down to 1, and counts the ways to arrange n different things in a row, such as 4! = 24.

points.title: Probability by counting arrangements
points.brief: Count the favourable arrangements and all the arrangements with the multiplication principle, then divide.

points.title: Judging how a study was run
points.brief: Ask how a study chose its sample, whether it had a control group, and how big it was, before trusting its findings.
